name: Travel_Systems
description: Ship-based travel between star systems, orbital mechanics, and planetary landing.

questions.question: Does travel teach real orbital mechanics and physics?
questions.answer: Yes. Orbital mechanics, gravity wells, fuel efficiency, and celestial navigation are real physics.

questions.question: Can the player learn about celestial navigation through travel?
questions.answer: Yes. Players navigate by star positions, planet orbits, and gravity slingshots. Real astronomy.

questions.question: Does fuel management teach real energy physics?
questions.answer: Yes. Fuel = energy. Different maneuvers cost different delta-v. Real rocket science principles.

questions.question: Can the player learn about gravity wells and escape velocity through gameplay?
questions.answer: Yes. Escaping a gravity well at different altitudes teaches real escape velocity physics.

questions.question: Is space travel visually impressive enough for marketing?
questions.answer: Yes. Space travel screenshots are inherently impressive.

questions.question: Does our travel system differ from other space games?
questions.answer: Our travel teaches real orbital mechanics. Most space games use fake physics for accessibility.

questions.question: Can orbital mechanics be a selling point?
questions.answer: Yes. Teaching real orbital mechanics through gameplay is a unique selling point.

questions.question: Do different star systems have different physical properties?

questions.question: What per-system travel costs (fuel, landing fees, port tariffs, hazard premiums) create route-level economics where low-cost shipping lanes compete with high-reward frontier routes?
questions.answer: Travel cost determines route profitability. A standard system hop costs 100 credits fuel + 25 landing fee + 5% cargo tariff. A frontier route costs 300 fuel + no landing fee + 20% hazard premium (piracy risk). The frontier must offer 4x margin to be worthwhile. Safe-core routes handle bulk low-margin goods; frontier routes carry high-value, low-volume goods.

questions.question: Does the travel system as a whole tell the story of a journey — from walking to flying to interstellar travel, each mode a chapter in the player's growing mastery of distance?
questions.answer: Travel tells the epic story: walking is the humble beginning, flying a ship is the first power-up, orbital mechanics is mastery, and interstellar navigation is transcendence — the modes of travel are the acts of the player's odyssey.

questions.question: Does interstellar travel balance spectacle (starfield transition, warp visual) with gameplay (fuel planning, navigation decisions, orbital insertion) so the player never feels like they're just watching a loading screen?
questions.answer: Warp is 3-8 seconds depending on distance, with star streak visual. During warp, fuel consumption rate is shown. Post-warp, the player must execute orbital insertion (no autopilot). Travel decisions (route, fuel stops, cargo weight) matter before every jump.

questions.question: Does the entire travel state (current system, current body, orbital parameters, fuel, plotted route) need to persist?
questions.answer: Yes. Travel state is the most complex persistent data: current star system ID, current orbital body, orbital position/velocity, fuel levels per tank, plotted route waypoints, navigation history. This is the heart of the game's persistent state. Written on manual save or significant travel event.

questions.question: Does interstellar travel model real astrophysics (relativistic time dilation, light-speed lag, gravitational lensing) or use gameplay-friendly warp mechanics?
questions.answer: Gameplay-friendly warp mechanics. Interstellar travel uses 'warp drive' (skip to destination after a loading screen with travel time calculation). No relativistic effects. In-system travel uses the orbital mechanics model (real physics). This split keeps interstellar travel accessible while teaching real orbital physics in-system.
